patient.chief_complaint: Confusion and unresponsiveness following brief convulsion 35 minutes ago, history of recent cardiac arrest
patient.history_present_illness: A 55-year-old White female accountant was brought to the emergency department by her husband after a brief generalized tonic-clonic seizure at home. The husband reports she convulsed for approximately 2 minutes and had not returned to her baseline level of alertness 35 minutes later. He was instructed to call 911. Critical history: the patient suffered a witnessed out-of-hospital cardiac arrest due to ventricular fibrillation 5 days ago. She was resuscitated after approximately 12 minutes of cardiac arrest (time from collapse to ROSC), intubated in the field, and was admitted to the cardiac ICU where she underwent targeted temperature management (TTM, 33°C for 24 hours) followed by controlled rewarming. She was extubated on day 3 and was discharged home on day 4 — somewhat prematurely in retrospect — with a newly implanted ICD. Since discharge she has been confused, more than expected, with prominent short-term memory impairment and episodes where she 'stares into space.' Her husband noted she had several brief 'staring spells' at home over the past 24 hours before today's convulsion. She takes aspirin, atorvastatin, and amiodarone following the cardiac arrest. Her husband reports the 'staring spells' were not recognized as seizures at discharge. No fever. No headache. No new cardiac symptoms. She was told post-cardiac arrest cognitive changes are 'normal' at discharge. Family history: mother with coronary artery disease. No epilepsy.

Continuous generalized periodic discharges (GPDs) with sharp triphasic components at 1.5-2.0 Hz, meeting electrographic criteria for non-convulsive status epilepticus, on a diffusely suppressed background. 2. Emerging burst-suppression pattern between ictal runs — bursts 1-3 seconds, interburst suppression 3-8 seconds. 3. Diffuse background suppression consistent with severe encephalopathy. output.impression: This is an ABNORMAL EEG. Compared to prior recording: 1. The burst-suppression pattern has evolved — interburst suppression now exceeds 6 seconds; bursts contain generalized periodic discharges with triphasic components. 2. Background reactivity is absent — no response to auditory or noxious stimulation. 3. Electrographic seizure activity is reduced compared to prior but remains present within bursts. This is a malignant EEG pattern in the post-cardiac arrest setting. Absent EEG reactivity and progressive burst-suppression are recognized as adverse prognostic EEG features
output.limitations: ICU artifact present. Sedation and temperature management may modify EEG background.

output.proposed: levetiracetam 1500 mg IV (new); amiodarone 200 mg daily (current); lacosamide (considered alternative AED)
interactions: Lacosamide + amiodarone: additive PR interval prolongation via complementary sodium channel blockade — increased risk of AV block; avoid combination
Levetiracetam + amiodarone: no clinically significant pharmacokinetic or pharmacodynamic interaction; levetiracetam does not affect cardiac conduction
Amiodarone + atorvastatin: amiodarone inhibits CYP3A4 and CYP2C9, increasing atorvastatin exposure — monitor for myopathy; already prescribed, no change needed
contraindications: Lacosamide in patients on amiodarone — additive PR prolongation and AV block risk
warnings: Use levetiracetam as first-line AED — safe with amiodarone, no conduction effects
Avoid lacosamide unless no alternatives — cardiac monitoring mandatory if used
Monitor ECG PR interval if any sodium-channel-blocking AED is introduced

output.impression: Bilateral absent N20 SSEP responses at greater than 24 hours post-cardiac arrest in the absence of confounders. Bilateral absent N20 is a recognized predictor of poor neurological prognosis after cardiac arrest; specificity approaches 100% in most published series when confounders are excluded. Clinical correlation recommended. Bilateral median nerve stimulation; recording from C3-Fz and C4-Fz; N20 cortical response evaluated. Bilateral absent N20 cortical responses — failure of somatosensory cortical signal transmission on both sides. Subcortical potentials (N14/P14) are present bilaterally, confirming adequate peripheral and subcortical conduction; the absence of N20 is cortical in origin. Bilateral absent N20 at greater than 24 hours post-cardiac arrest, in the absence of confounders (sedation, hypothermia at recording time, metabolic disturbance), has been associated with a high specificity for poor neurological outcome in published series

results.title: Neuroprognostication after cardiac arrest: systematic review and meta-analysis
results.key_finding: Multimodal neuroprognostication: bilateral absent SSEPs (specificity 100%), NSE >33 mcg/L at 48-72h (specificity >90%), extensive bilateral cortical DWI restriction on MRI, and malignant EEG patterns (burst-suppression, suppression) together predict very poor neurological outcome (death/VS) with near 100% specificity. Post-anoxic NCSE alone is not invariably fatal but combined with other markers indicates poor prognosis.

output.summary: Multimodal neuroprognostication after cardiac arrest combines EEG, MRI, somatosensory evoked potentials, and serum biomarkers (NSE). Bilateral absent N20 SSEPs have been reported with approximately 100% specificity for poor neurological outcome in multiple meta-analyses, provided confounders are excluded. NSE greater than 33 mcg/L at 48-72 hours has been reported with greater than 90% specificity for poor outcome. Extensive bilateral cortical DWI restriction on MRI and malignant EEG patterns (burst-suppression with absent reactivity, generalized suppression) are additional unfavorable prognostic markers. The combination of multiple adverse markers increases prognostic certainty but multimodal assessment is recommended before clinical decisions. Post-anoxic non-convulsive status epilepticus as an isolated finding is not invariably fatal.
